events.title: Classical Greece: From Marathon to Socrates
events.summary: In 490 BC a small Athenian army beat the mighty Persian Empire at Marathon, 300 Spartans held the pass at Thermopylae, and the Greek fleet crushed Persia at Salamis. Free Athens then blossomed: Pericles built the Parthenon, citizens voted on laws, and thinkers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle asked questions we still argue about, until a long war with Sparta ended the golden age.
events.why: Later painters used Greece as a picture of what free people can do. David showed Leonidas and Socrates as models of courage, and Raphael painted all the great philosophers together in one room to say the Renaissance was ancient Athens reborn.

items.note: Three hundred Spartans hold the pass while the Persian army pours toward them. David painted the calm before the last stand, with the warriors combing their hair for battle.
According to legend, a runner named Pheidippides raced from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens to announce that the Greeks had beaten the Persians, then collapsed and died.
Wilhelm von Kaulbach shows the sea battle of 480 BC in which the Greek ships crushed the Persian fleet of King Xerxes in the narrow waters near Athens.
Socrates, sentenced by Athens in 399 BC, calmly reaches for the cup of poison while his friends fall apart.
The sculptor Phidias shows Pericles and a circle of Athenian friends the carved marble frieze made for the Parthenon, the great temple on the Acropolis.
Raphael filled a Vatican room with the great thinkers of ancient Greece: Plato points up at the sky of ideas while Aristotle holds out a hand toward the Earth.
The philosopher Socrates teaches the young Alcibiades, a brilliant and very spoiled Athenian aristocrat who later became a famous general and then a traitor.
Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg paints the wise old Socrates and the handsome young Alcibiades in the Athens of the 400s BC.
Guests recline at a dinner party in ancient Athens, taking turns to give speeches about love, in a scene from Plato's dialogue The Symposium.
A terrible illness has struck an ancient city and people are dying in the streets.
The philosopher Aristotle, dressed in rich 1600s clothes, rests a hand on a bust of the poet Homer and seems lost in thought about wisdom, fame and money.
Miltiades, the Athenian general who won at Marathon, died in disgrace, and his son Cimon agreed to take his place in prison so that his father could have a proper funeral.
The Parthenon, the temple built in the golden age of Athens in the 400s BC, stands in golden light on the Acropolis.
Vasily Polenov, a Russian painter, shows the ruined Parthenon standing high above Athens, the temple Pericles built in the golden age.

events.title: Alexander the Great
events.summary: Alexander of Macedon became king at twenty and, in just twelve years, conquered Persia, Egypt and lands as far as India without losing a major battle. He spread Greek language and ideas across the known world, then died in Babylon at thirty-two. His generals split his empire, but Greek culture lived on in it for centuries.
events.why: Alexander is the model of the young hero-conqueror. Painters showed him taming his horse Bucephalus, cutting the Gordian knot and being kind to his enemy's captured family, scenes that mix glory with mercy.

items.note: Alexander calmly drinks the medicine his doctor Philip offers, even after being warned that Philip might be poisoning him, a famous story about trust.
Thousands of tiny soldiers swarm across a landscape of mountains, sea and glowing sky in Albrecht Altdorfer's view of Alexander the Great beating the Persian king Darius at Issus in 333 BC.
Alexander rides into Babylon on a chariot in 331 BC with elephants, flower petals and cheering crowds.
Alexander's cavalry charges across the Granicus river in 334 BC, the first big battle against the Persians.
The Indian king Porus, who fought bravely and lost, is brought before Alexander.
After the Battle of Issus, the mother and family of the defeated Persian king kneel before Alexander.
Pietro da Cortona paints a whirlwind of horses and spears as Alexander charges at the Persian king Darius.
Jan Brueghel the Elder spreads thousands of tiny soldiers across a sunlit plain for the battle that ended the Persian Empire, probably Alexander's win over King Darius.
Alexander the Great, who has everything, offers the philosopher Diogenes anything he wants.
According to legend, whoever could untie the huge Gordian knot would rule Asia.
Alexander the Great sits with Roxane, the Bactrian princess he married in 327 BC.

events.title: Founding of Rome & the Early Republic
events.summary: Rome began, so the legend goes, when twin brothers Romulus and Remus, raised by a wolf, founded a city on seven hills in 753 BC. After the last king was thrown out, Rome became a Republic run by elected leaders. Stories of heroic early Romans taught later generations what it meant to be a good citizen.
events.why: In the 1700s, painters like David and Poussin used these Roman tales to show duty, sacrifice and loyalty to your country. The pictures were also political: they said the people, not a king, should rule.

items.note: Three brothers swear to fight for Rome, while the women weep. David used this legend of early Roman duty to say that citizens must put their country first.
The Sabine women throw themselves between the armies of their husbands and their fathers to stop the fighting.
Brutus, who helped found the Roman Republic, has condemned his own sons for plotting to bring back the king.
According to Roman legend, the twin babies Romulus and Remus were left by a river and fed by a she-wolf until a shepherd found them.
A young Roman woman named Cloelia, held hostage by the Etruscan king Porsena, escapes and leads other hostages across the Tiber river.
The legendary Roman soldier Horatius Cocles holds a bridge alone against an enemy army while his friends chop it down behind him.
The Roman farmer Cincinnatus is called from his field in 458 BC and made dictator to save the city, then gives up power after only a few days and goes back to his farm.
The Roman general Coriolanus, exiled by his own city, marches on Rome with an enemy army, but his mother and wife beg him to stop and he turns back.
The shepherd Faustulus brings the two baby twins, found beside the wolf, home to his wife to raise.
A shepherd family takes in the twin babies who will one day found Rome, in a calm, sunlit scene full of warm colors.
Lucretia, a noble Roman woman, stands with a dagger after a terrible wrong, and according to legend her death made the Romans drive out their last king in 509 BC and create the Republic.
In Roman legend the young city of Rome had no wives, so Romulus's men carried off the women of the neighboring Sabine tribe.

events.title: Hannibal & the Punic Wars
events.summary: Rome and Carthage, a great trading city in North Africa, fought three wars between 264 and 146 BC. The Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army with war elephants over the Alps and crushed the Romans at Cannae, but Rome never gave up. In the end Scipio beat Hannibal and Rome destroyed Carthage, becoming master of the Mediterranean.
events.why: Hannibal's elephants crossing the Alps is one of history's most dramatic scenes. Artists like Turner used it to show how small people look against nature and fate.

items.note: Turner paints Hannibal's army swallowed by a swirling Alpine blizzard, his way of showing how small people are against nature.
Goya's early painting shows Hannibal gazing down on Italy after leading elephants and soldiers over the Alps.
Turner imagines Carthage, Rome's great rival, rising as a shining harbor city under its legendary queen Dido.
The boy Hannibal swears at an altar to hate Rome forever, with his father Hamilcar watching.
At the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal's army surrounded and crushed a larger Roman army, one of the greatest defeats in Roman history.
The Roman general Scipio Africanus returns a captured young bride to her fiancé instead of keeping her as a prize, a famous story about self-control.
The same story of fairness in war: Scipio hands a captive woman back to her fiancé.
Giovanni Bellini painted this long, stone-colored picture around 1506 to look like an ancient Roman carved frieze, telling a story of Scipio's mercy.
Hannibal's elephants and soldiers struggle over a steep snowy pass in the Alps in 218 BC on their way to attack Rome.
A long Renaissance chest-panel shows the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, where Scipio finally beat Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War.
A crowded engraving of the Battle of Zama, where Scipio defeated Hannibal in 202 BC.

events.title: Julius Caesar & the Fall of the Roman Republic
events.summary: Julius Caesar won Gaul, crossed the Rubicon river in 49 BC with his army, beat his rival Pompey and made himself dictator of Rome. Many senators feared he wanted to be king, and on the Ides of March in 44 BC a group of them stabbed him to death. The civil wars that followed ended the Roman Republic for good.
events.why: Few events have been painted so often. Artists were fascinated by Caesar's fall: the moment when power, friendship and fear all collided in a single room.

items.note: Gérôme leaves Caesar's body on the floor of the Senate while the killers walk away, a quiet and chilling view of the Ides of March.
Camuccini shows the senators closing in on Caesar, with the statue of Pompey looking on.
A young Cleopatra is delivered to Caesar rolled in a carpet. This meeting started a famous alliance.
On the Ides of March in 44 BC, Roman senators, including Caesar's friend Brutus, stabbed Julius Caesar in the Senate.
In 63 BC the great speaker Cicero stands and accuses Catiline of plotting against Rome, and the other senators move away from him.
The Gaulish chief Vercingetorix surrenders to Julius Caesar in 52 BC after the siege of Alesia, ending a big revolt against Rome.
The Roman general Marius, hiding from enemies in a marsh, stares down the soldier sent to kill him, who drops his sword.
The exiled Roman general Marius sits alone among the ruins of Carthage, a symbol of how quickly fortune changes.
Fulvia, the fierce wife of Mark Antony, takes revenge on the dead Cicero, the great speaker who had attacked her husband, in this gruesome scene from the civil wars after Caesar's death.
Julius Caesar, stabbed by senators on the Ides of March in 44 BC, falls at the foot of the statue of his old rival Pompey.

events.title: Cleopatra, Antony & the Rise of the Empire
events.summary: After Caesar died, his adopted son Octavian fought Mark Antony, who had joined forces with Cleopatra, the last queen of Egypt. Octavian won the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, Egypt became part of Rome, and he became Augustus, the first Roman emperor. His reign started two hundred years of peace known as the Pax Romana.
events.why: Cleopatra's story mixes love, power and tragedy, which made it a favorite subject for painters from the Baroque era onward. Many pictures show her as glamorous; real Cleopatra was a brilliant ruler who spoke many languages.

items.note: In 41 BC Cleopatra of Egypt arrives to meet the Roman general Mark Antony and wins him over with a spectacular show.
Before Antony there was Caesar: Gérôme shows the young queen arriving in Caesar's rooms.
Cleopatra, near the end of her rule, studies how poisons work by watching their effect on prisoners.
Etty paints Cleopatra arriving by barge at Tarsus to meet Mark Antony, the famous start of their alliance.
In Tiepolo's glittering scene, Cleopatra dissolves a priceless pearl in her wine to win a bet with Antony.
Augustus, the first emperor, listens as the poet Virgil reads from the Aeneid, the epic that celebrates Rome's origins.
The poet Virgil reads from his epic poem the Aeneid to the emperor Augustus and his sister Octavia, who faints at the lines about her dead son Marcellus.
Dozens of oared warships crash together at Actium in 31 BC, the sea battle where Octavian's fleet beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra.
Claude Lorrain turns the arrival of Cleopatra at Tarsus into a glowing harbor scene, where the Egyptian queen steps ashore to meet Mark Antony in the golden light of sunrise.
Jean-Léon Gérôme shows peoples from across the Roman Empire bowing before Augustus in Rome, at the moment of peace in which, according to Christian tradition, Jesus was born.
Cleopatra bets Mark Antony that she can spend a fortune on one dinner, then drops a priceless pearl in her wine and drinks it.

events.title: Imperial Rome & Pompeii
events.summary: At its height the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt, with roads, aqueducts, theaters and the giant Colosseum, where gladiators fought in front of tens of thousands. In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum, freezing everyday Roman life in ash for almost 1,700 years.
events.why: The 1800s were mad about Rome. Painters like Lawrence Alma-Tadema made super-detailed pictures of Roman daily life, using what archaeologists were digging up at Pompeii.

items.note: Mount Vesuvius erupts in 79 AD as the people of Pompeii run for their lives beneath a rain of ash.
A victorious gladiator waits for the crowd's verdict on his fallen rival. The painting made Gérôme famous.
A teenage emperor smothers his dinner guests under falling rose petals, a picture of Roman excess.
The philosopher Seneca, forced by Nero to take his own life, calmly says goodbye to his friends.
Eckersberg paints the broken Colosseum, once the stage of gladiator games, glowing in Roman sunlight.
After the emperor Caligula was killed in AD 41, soldiers found his uncle Claudius hiding behind a curtain and made him emperor.
Titus's soldiers parade through Rome in AD 71 with treasure from the conquest of Jerusalem.
The Roman emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius, dying, presents his young son Commodus to his friends and asks them to guide him, though Commodus turned out to be a bad emperor.
Gladiators salute the emperor with the words 'we who are about to die salute you' before a fight in the Roman arena.
Thomas Cole paints the half-ruined Colosseum glowing in the Roman sun in 1832, the great arena of the emperors now open to the sky.
John Martin's glowing sky and lightning show the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 that buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.
The Dutch painter Maarten van Heemskerck shows himself in front of the Colosseum in 1553, when the great arena was already a crumbling ruin.
Hubert Robert paints the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64 with a river-bridge silhouetted against the flames.
The emperor Nero, who has just had his own mother Agrippina killed, lies on a couch filled with guilt while his attendants look away.
J.
In AD 70 the Roman army under the future emperor Titus destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem at the end of a Jewish revolt.

events.title: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.summary: In the 300s and 400s AD, the Western Roman Empire was weakened by civil wars, money troubles and pressure from peoples like the Goths, Vandals and Huns. Rome itself was sacked in 410 and 455, and in 476 the last emperor in the West was removed. The Eastern Empire, called Byzantium, carried on for another thousand years.
events.why: Artists have used Rome's fall as a warning ever since. In The Course of Empire, Thomas Cole showed a great city rising and falling, and told Americans that no nation is safe forever.

items.note: In 455 AD the Vandal king Genseric captured Rome and looted it for two weeks, one of the blows that weakened the Western Empire.
In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric broke into Rome, the first time in about 800 years that an enemy had taken the city.
Attila the Hun, whose army terrified Rome in the 450s, rides over Italy, trampling art and learning under his horses' hooves.
In 452 Pope Leo I met Attila the Hun and, according to the story, persuaded him to turn his army back from Rome.
Ulpiano Checa, who loved painting wild horses and chariots, shows hordes of mounted warriors charging across a snowy plain.
Attila the Hun feasts with his warriors and advisors in a great hall.
The emperor Constantine rides into Rome in 312 AD after beating his rival at the Milvian Bridge, an event that opened the way for Christianity to become the empire's main religion.
Constantine's army defeats his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD, a victory he said was helped by a vision of a cross.
The weak emperor Honorius was told that Rome had fallen and said it couldn't be, he had just fed her.
The Visigoth king Alaric enters Athens in 396 AD, and the city's people stand before him in fear.
Constantius, a Roman emperor, names his son Constantine as his successor in 306 AD, and Constantine goes on to become the first Christian emperor.
In 390 Bishop Ambrose of Milan stands in the church doorway and refuses to let the Emperor Theodosius enter until he repents for a terrible massacre.

events.title: Charlemagne & the Early Middle Ages
events.summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks, ruled much of Western Europe from 768 to 814. On Christmas Day in 800, the Pope crowned him emperor in Rome, the first in the West since Rome's fall. He supported scholars and schools, and his court helped save many ancient books.
events.why: Painters showed Charlemagne as the founder of Christian Europe: a wise king surrounded by scholars and knights. In the 1800s he became a national hero for both the French and the Germans.

items.note: In 732 the Frankish leader Charles Martel stopped a Muslim army from advancing farther into France at the Battle of Tours and Poitiers, and his grandson was Charlemagne.
Clovis, king of the Franks, vows to become a Christian if he wins at Tolbiac against the Alemanni, and then he does.
The hero Roland, one of Charlemagne's knights, dies after fighting at Roncesvalles in 778, in the legend that became the Song of Roland.
Pepin the Short, Charlemagne's father, finally takes the city of Narbonne in 759, driving out the Muslim garrison.
Clovis, the king of the Franks, is baptized by a bishop around the year 496, which made France a Christian kingdom.
On Christmas Day in 800, Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome, the first emperor in the West in over 300 years.
This glowing little picture of Charlemagne's crowning comes from the Grandes Chroniques de France, the French royal history.
Workers build the great chapel at Aachen, Charlemagne's capital, using ladders and stone blocks.
Master Theodoric, the court painter to Emperor Charles IV in Prague, painted Charlemagne as a saint in the 1360s.
The emperor Charlemagne and his son Louis the Pious stand side by side in a manuscript illumination from a French royal chronicle of the 1300s or 1400s.

events.title: The Viking Age
events.summary: From about 793 to 1066, Norse sailors from Norway, Denmark and Sweden set out in their longships to raid, trade and settle. They reached England, France, Russia and Iceland, and Leif Erikson's crew landed in North America around the year 1000. Their sagas, gods and ships still capture the imagination.
events.why: Norwegian and Scandinavian painters of the 1800s used the Viking age to say who they were as new nations. Their pictures of Harald Fairhair, Leif Erikson and Odin's hunt made the sagas look as real as yesterday.

items.note: Leif Erikson's crew, sailing west from Greenland around the year 1000, see the shores of North America for the first time.
Arbo shows the Norse god Odin riding across the stormy sky with his ghostly hunters.
A Valkyrie, one of Odin's warrior-maidens in Norse myth, gallops over the battlefield to choose the bravest fighters.
Thor swings his hammer at the giants in a story every Viking child knew.
King Olav II falls at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030.
In 1066 King Harald Hardrada of Norway, the last great Viking king, is killed in a battle against the English at Stamford Bridge.
Harald Fairhair wins the sea battle of Hafrsfjord around the year 872, a victory the sagas say united Norway under one king.
At the sea battle of Svolder in the year 1000, King Olav Tryggvason's famous ship the Long Serpent was surrounded by enemy ships.
Olav Tryggvason sails back to Norway in 995 to take the throne, and the sagas say he then pushed his people to become Christian.
The conquered king Gryting is brought before Harald Fairhair in a scene from the Viking sagas.
Viking-age traders, called Varangians, sail a dragon-headed ship into a Slavic harbor in this glowing scene.
According to a saga, King Olav Tryggvason asks the proud Swedish queen Sigrid to marry him and become Christian, she refuses, and he strikes her with his glove.
The famous Viking hero Ragnar Lodbrok sits beside his clever wife Kráka in this scene from the Norse sagas.

events.title: The Norman Conquest
events.summary: In 1066 the Norman duke William crossed the English Channel and defeated King Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings. William became king of England and the Normans built castles, changed the law and brought French words to the English language. The famous Bayeux Tapestry tells the story in stitches.
events.why: The year 1066 is the most famous date in English history. Victorian painters made scenes of Harold's death and William's landing to show where England's story began.

items.note: Harold, the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, dies at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
Norman knights on horses and archers charge in this section of the Bayeux Tapestry, the embroidered story of the conquest of England in 1066.
Harold takes the throne of England in January 1066 after King Edward dies, in a scene from the Bayeux Tapestry.
Harold swears an oath of loyalty to William of Normandy with his hands on holy relics, in a scene from the Bayeux Tapestry.
The Bayeux Tapestry begins with the old, childless King Edward the Confessor of England on his throne, whose death would lead to the fight for the crown in 1066.
Horses tumble and soldiers fight at the Battle of Hastings in the Bayeux Tapestry.
William of Normandy gives Harold weapons in this scene from the Bayeux Tapestry.
Duke William of Normandy sits with his half-brothers, Bishop Odo and Robert, planning the invasion of England.
In the early 1800s the English antiquarian Charles Alfred Stothard made careful copies of the Bayeux Tapestry for the Society of Antiquaries.
Lady Godiva, who lived in the years before the Norman Conquest, rides through Coventry to win a tax cut for the townspeople.
Edmund Blair Leighton shows Lady Godiva before her famous ride through Coventry, which in the legend she made to persuade her husband to lower the town's taxes.
The legend says Lady Godiva of Coventry agreed to ride through the town to persuade her husband to cut the taxes, while the people promised to stay inside.

events.title: The Crusades
events.summary: Beginning in 1095, European armies marched east to capture Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Over about 200 years there were many crusades, with famous leaders like Richard the Lionheart and Saladin. They changed trade, travel and ideas between Europe and the Middle East, but caused great suffering too.
events.why: Romantic painters of the 1800s loved the Crusades as tales of knights and faraway adventures, often prettier than the real history. Looking closely, you can ask: whose side is the painter showing?

items.note: Crusaders ride into Constantinople in 1204, in a scene that shows how the crusades could turn on fellow Christians.
In 1212 thousands of European children, many in poor families, set off on a march to the Holy Land, and most never got there.
The Norman leader Bohemond climbs the walls of Antioch in 1098 in one of the crusaders' most daring moments.
The aged and blind Doge of Venice, Enrico Dandolo, speaks in front of the cathedral to stir up the Fourth Crusade.
Baldwin of Boulogne, a leader of the First Crusade, is welcomed into the city of Edessa in 1098, where he became its ruler and founded the first Crusader state.
Richard the Lionheart of England fights in the siege of Acre during the Third Crusade, in 1191.
In 1204 crusaders on the Fourth Crusade attacked the Christian city of Constantinople from their ships instead of going to the Holy Land.
In 1095 Pope Urban II gives a famous speech at Clermont that started the First Crusade, and the crowd shouts 'God wills it!' This illustration comes from a French manuscript made around 1474.
Saladin, the great Muslim leader who recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, meets Guy of Lusignan, the king of Jerusalem he had defeated at Hattin.
Jacopo Tintoretto paints the Venetians and crusaders capturing Constantinople in 1204 as a dark swirl of fighting.
King Louis IX of France, called Saint Louis, rides on a rearing horse.
In 1229 Emperor Frederick II made a treaty with Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt, which gave Jerusalem back to the Christians without a battle.
After the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart was captured on his way home and held for ransom by the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI, who finally pardoned him.

events.title: The Hundred Years' War & Joan of Arc
events.summary: From 1337 to 1453 England and France fought on and off in the Hundred Years' War. English archers won at Crécy and Agincourt, but a teenage peasant girl named Joan of Arc rallied the French and helped crown King Charles VII. By the end, England had lost almost all of its French lands.
events.why: Joan of Arc became a saint and a national hero, so painters of the 1800s showed her as everything from a quiet farm girl hearing voices to a shining warrior on horseback.

items.note: Joan of Arc, a teenage peasant girl who said saints told her to save France, rides into battle with her banner to lift the siege of Orléans in 1429.
On May 8, 1429 Joan of Arc rides into Orléans as a hero after the English siege is broken, and the crowd cheers her.
Eugène Thirion shows Joan of Arc, in a simple red dress, listening to the angels and saints whose voices, she said, told her to save France.
Joan of Arc stands before her judges at her trial in 1431, after she was captured by the English allies.
A walled city is attacked with cannons and ladders in this illuminated manuscript showing the siege of Orléans in 1428–1429, the turning point of the Hundred Years' War.
King Henry V of England, with a small tired army, waits for the French on the morning of the Battle of Agincourt in 1415.
This medieval chronicle picture of the Battle of Agincourt in 1415 was painted only a few years after the battle itself, in the chronicle of the monk Thomas Walsingham.
The sixteen-year-old Edward, called the Black Prince, stands among the dead after the Battle of Crécy in 1346, where English archers beat the French.
At Poitiers in 1356 the English army led by the Black Prince defeated the French and captured their king, John II.
King Edward III embraces his young son the Black Prince after the Battle of Crécy in 1346, proud of his first big victory.
After winning at Poitiers, the Black Prince treats the captured French king John with great courtesy.
English longbowmen face French knights and crossbowmen in a colorful scene from the chronicles of Jean Froissart, the great historian of the Hundred Years' War.

events.title: The Black Death
events.summary: In 1347 a terrible plague reached Europe on trading ships and killed perhaps a third of the people in about four years. Villages emptied, and the world changed: workers were suddenly scarce, so they could ask for higher pay. Art filled up with skeletons, dances of death and prayers for mercy.
events.why: People then had no idea what caused the disease, so artists painted it as a mysterious visitor: Death himself walking among the living. These pictures are reminders of how fragile life seemed.

items.note: An army of skeletons sweeps across a ruined land, killing kings and peasants alike.
People in a plague-struck city pray to Saint Sebastian, who was believed to protect against the disease, while angels and demons hover above.
Skeletons dance with the living in this woodcut from the Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493.
Death, a skeleton, leads the emperor away from his throne in one of Hans Holbein the Younger's Dance of Death woodcuts.
A skeleton gently takes a cardinal by the robe in one of Holbein's Dance of Death woodcuts.
A plague doctor wears a long coat and a mask with a beak that was stuffed with herbs, to try to keep disease away.
A long painted frieze shows skeletons leading people of every rank in a dance toward the grave.
Death, a skeleton on a winged creature, swoops over a plague-stricken city in this chilling painting.
A terrible illness has struck an ancient city and people are dying in the streets.
Skeletons lead a long line of kings, bishops, merchants and peasants toward the grave in this wall painting in a tiny church in Slovenia.
A knight in armor rides calmly through a dark valley while Death with an hourglass and a horned Devil follow behind him.
A dying miser lies in bed while Death stands in the doorway and a demon tempts him with a bag of money.
The painter pauses at his easel, as a skeleton with a one-stringed fiddle whispers in his ear.
Christ appoints Saint Roch as the protector of plague victims, a saint who was believed to have cared for the sick during an epidemic.

events.title: Byzantium & the Fall of Constantinople
events.summary: For a thousand years after Rome fell in the West, the Byzantine Empire ruled from Constantinople (now Istanbul), a golden city with the great church of Hagia Sophia. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured it after a long siege. The fall of Constantinople is often used to mark the end of the Middle Ages.
events.why: To artists, Constantinople stood for a dazzling lost world. Painters showed emperors, empresses and the mighty walls that held out for so long.

items.note: Ottoman ships crowd the water around the walled city of Constantinople in this manuscript painting of the siege of 1453.
Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 when he was only 21, and later he asked Venice to send a painter to his court.
Sultan Mehmed II rides in triumph through the gates of Constantinople after its fall in 1453, with red banners overhead.
The Ottoman army marches toward Constantinople in 1453 in a painting by Fausto Zonaro, an Italian artist who worked for the Ottoman sultans.
Belisarius, the great general of the Byzantine emperor Justinian, is said in a legend to have ended his life blind and begging, and here a soldier who once served under him recognizes him.
A Greek folk-style painting shows the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 like a map, with soldiers and ships all around the city.
Ottoman soldiers with ladders and cannon storm the walls in this French manuscript painting of the fall of Constantinople in 1453, made only a few years afterward.
In a golden mosaic in the church of Hagia Sophia, the Byzantine Empress Zoe and her husband Constantine IX stand on each side of Christ and offer gifts.
Christ looks out from the Deësis mosaic of Hagia Sophia, with the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist on either side.
The Virgin Mary and Child with the Emperor John II Komnenos and the Empress Irene, in a glittering golden mosaic in Hagia Sophia made around 1118.
John Singer Sargent paints the soaring inside of the great church of Hagia Sophia, built by Justinian in 537 and turned into a mosque after the Ottoman conquest of 1453.

A domed fountain stands at the gate of the old palace of the Ottoman sultans in Constantinople, in a drawing by the English artist John Frederick Lewis, who traveled through the Ottoman capital in the 1830s and 1840s.

events.title: The Renaissance
events.summary: In the 1400s and 1500s Italian cities like Florence became bursting with new ideas. Rich families like the Medici paid for artists and scholars who studied ancient Greece and Rome, discovered how to paint perspective, and made science, books and art flourish. The printing press helped the new ideas spread across Europe.
events.why: The Renaissance was one of the most art-filled times in history. These pictures show the artists, patrons and thinkers who changed the world, from artists' own times and from later painters who looked back in awe.

items.note: Ingres imagines Leonardo, in his last days in France, dying in the arms of King Francis I, a picture of the friendship between artists and rulers.
The Mona Lisa's soft, mysterious smile and misty background make her the most famous painting in the world.
Leonardo painted the moment Jesus tells his twelve friends that one of them will betray him, and each gesture shows a different reaction.
God stretches out a finger toward Adam, and the tiny gap between their hands has become one of the most famous images ever.
Raphael filled a Vatican room with the great thinkers of ancient Greece: Plato points up at the sky of ideas while Aristotle holds out a hand toward the Earth.
The goddess Venus arrives on the shore on a giant seashell, blown by the winds, in Botticelli's most famous painting of about 1485.
Leonardo's famous drawing of a man with arms and legs stretched inside a circle and a square shows the ideal human proportions described by the Roman architect Vitruvius.
Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine thinker who wrote The Prince, a book about how rulers really get and keep power.
Cosimo de' Medici the Elder was the banker who made his family the rulers of Florence, and he paid for libraries, churches and artists.
Botticelli painted the Three Kings visiting Jesus and gave the kings the faces of the Medici family, the rulers of Florence, and put himself in the crowd.
Girolamo Savonarola was a fiery preacher who held Florence in his grip in the 1490s, burning books, mirrors and paintings in his Bonfire of the Vanities.
Girolamo Savonarola, the preacher who ruled Florence for a few years, is hanged and burned in the main square in 1498 after losing the support of the people.
A young woman, Cecilia Gallerani, holds a white ermine, which was a symbol of purity, in one of Leonardo's few portraits of a woman.
The poet Dante, in exile from Florence, passes some women in Verona while they whisper that he has been to hell, a joke on his great poem the Inferno.

events.title: Columbus & the Age of Discovery
events.summary: In 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain and reached the Caribbean. Over the next hundred years, Portuguese, Spanish, English and French explorers like da Gama, Magellan and Cortés crossed oceans and met peoples who had never been in contact with Europe. The Age of Discovery connected the world, but it also brought conquest, disease and hardship for Indigenous peoples.
events.why: Artists of the 1800s made these voyages look like grand adventures. Today we can also ask who is missing from the picture and what the people who already lived there would have shown.

items.note: Columbus steps ashore in the Caribbean in 1492, planting the Spanish flag. Painted 350 years later, it shows how Americans imagined the moment.
Columbus argues his plan to sail west before skeptical scholars.
Christopher Columbus, poor and worn out, stops with his young son at a monastery in Spain, where a friendly prior helps him get a hearing at the court of Queen Isabella.
Columbus sits alone beside the sea, lost in dreams of the voyage west that will change the world.
The Spanish conqueror Hernán Cortés and the Aztec ruler Montezuma meet in the great city of Tenochtitlan in 1519, followed by war.
In 1532 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa, beginning the Spanish conquest of the Inca empire.
The Virgin Mary spreads her cloak over sailors, explorers and ships in an altarpiece painted for the Spanish House of Trade in Seville in about 1535.
A huge Portuguese trading ship sails into a golden Japanese harbor, with people in strange foreign clothes.
Francis Drake rests his hand on a globe in a portrait celebrating his voyage around the world from 1577 to 1580, the first by an English captain.
The English explorer Henry Hudson sails up what is now the Hudson River in 1609 and meets the Lenape people on the shore.
Henry Hudson, his son and a few others sit in a small boat in the icy northern sea after the crew turned against him in 1611 and cast them adrift.
The explorer Amerigo Vespucci stands in front of a woman who stands for America, newly awakened, in an allegorical engraving by Stradanus of about 1589.
This famous portrait is said to show Christopher Columbus, but it was painted by Sebastiano del Piombo in 1519, years after Columbus died, and no one knows what the explorer really looked like.
Hernán Cortés, the Spanish conqueror who led the fall of the Aztec empire in 1519 to 1521, in a 19th-century portrait by the Mexican painter José Salomé Pina.

events.title: The Protestant Reformation
events.summary: In 1517 a German monk named Martin Luther challenged the Church by posting his 95 Theses. With the help of the printing press, his ideas spread fast and Europe split into Catholic and Protestant lands. The Reformation changed religion, politics, education and even who could read the Bible.
events.why: Protestant painters like Lucas Cranach made Luther's portrait famous in his own lifetime, and later artists painted dramatic scenes such as Luther standing alone before the Emperor at Worms.

items.note: In 1521 Martin Luther stands in front of the Emperor Charles V in Worms and refuses to take back his writings, saying 'Here I stand.' Anton von Werner painted this scene in 1877 as a founding moment of the Reformation.
Martin Luther, the monk who challenged the Church, in a portrait painted in 1528 by his friend Lucas Cranach the Elder.
Martin Luther and his friend and fellow reformer Philipp Melanchthon, shown side by side in two matching panels painted by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1543.
According to tradition, on October 31, 1517, Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses, complaints against the Church's sale of pardons, to the church door in Wittenberg, which launched the Reformation.
Philipp Melanchthon, the teacher and thinker who became Luther's closest partner in the Reformation, in an engraving by Albrecht Dürer from 1526.
Erasmus, the Dutch scholar who wrote with wit about the Church's faults, sits writing in this calm portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger of 1523.
Henry VIII, in a puffed gold and jeweled jacket, stands with his hands on his hips in this Holbein portrait of 1537.
Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury who helped Henry VIII break with Rome and wrote the English Book of Common Prayer, was burned at the stake in 1556 under Queen Mary.
Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's chief minister, carried out the king's break with Rome and closed England's monasteries, but he fell from power and was executed in 1540.
In 1520 King Henry VIII of England and King Francis I of France met near Calais in a huge display of tents, banquets and tournaments, each trying to look richer than the other.
Bishops fill a great hall at the Council of Trent, held between 1545 and 1563 to answer the Protestant Reformation and reform the Catholic Church.
King Henry VIII meets Anne Boleyn in a palace hall, the beginning of the romance that led him to break with the Catholic Church.
Catherine of Aragon kneels before her husband Henry VIII at a church court in 1529, begging him not to end their marriage.
Pope Paul III, the pope who called the Council of Trent and approved the new Jesuit order, in a portrait painted by Titian in 1543.

events.title: Elizabeth I & the Spanish Armada
events.summary: Elizabeth I ruled England from 1558 to 1603, a time of explorers, theater and Shakespeare. In 1588 King Philip II of Spain sent a huge fleet, the Armada, to invade England, but smaller English ships and fierce storms scattered it. The victory made England a sea power.
events.why: Elizabeth's portraits were carefully designed to make her look powerful and almost magical. The famous Armada Portrait uses symbols and clothes to say: England rules the waves.

items.note: Queen Elizabeth I rests her hand on a globe, a symbol that she ruled the seas, while behind her are scenes of the Spanish Armada's defeat in 1588.
English fireships drift into the Spanish fleet at night in 1588 and the great Armada scatters in a blaze of flames.
A crowd of English and Spanish ships sail in the crescent formation of the Spanish Armada in this painting made not long after the battle of 1588.
Elizabeth I, about 70 years old, holds a rainbow and wears a cloak covered in eyes and ears, a symbol of how much she saw.
Elizabeth I in a huge white ruff and jeweled gown, painted around 1595 by Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger.
Elizabeth I is carried in a grand procession by her courtiers and noblemen, like the center of a parade.
Philip II, King of Spain, as a young prince in glittering armor and white hose.
Mary I, queen of England from 1553 to 1558, tried to bring England back to the Catholic Church and was nicknamed 'Bloody Mary' by her enemies.
Mary, Queen of Scots, was Elizabeth I's cousin and rival, held prisoner in England for 19 years before she was beheaded in 1587.
Francis Drake rests his hand on a globe in a portrait celebrating his voyage around the world from 1577 to 1580, the first by an English captain.
Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth I's spymaster, uncovered plots against the queen, including the one that led to the downfall of Mary, Queen of Scots.
The old queen sits on cushions on the floor of her room, refusing to go to bed, while her courtiers watch anxiously.
Eighteen-year-old Mary, Queen of Scots, stands on a ship leaving the shores of France in 1561, where she grew up, to return to Scotland.

events.title: The Thirty Years' War & the Dutch Revolt
events.summary: The Dutch rebelled against Spanish rule from 1568 and the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) spread across Germany and beyond, one of Europe's deadliest conflicts. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended both wars, made the Dutch Republic independent and started the modern idea of countries with borders.
events.why: Some artists painted heroic generals; others, like Callot, showed how terrible war really is. Spain's Velázquez painted a famous scene of a defeated Dutch commander handing over the keys, with surprising kindness.

items.note: The Dutch governor hands the keys of the city of Breda to the Spanish general Spinola in 1625, and Spinola kindly stops him from kneeling.
Delegates from Spain and the Dutch Republic raise their hands to swear to the peace treaty of 1648 that ended the Eighty Years' War.
In 1620 the Catholic army defeated the Protestant Bohemian forces outside Prague on the White Mountain, an early victory in the Thirty Years' War.
In 1618 angry Protestant nobles threw two Catholic officials out of a window of Prague Castle.
Armies clash across a wide plain at the Battle of Lützen in 1632, where the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus won the battle but was killed.
An army attacks the German city of Magdeburg in 1631, one of the worst moments of the Thirty Years' War, when most of the city was destroyed.
Members of Amsterdam's civic guard celebrate the Peace of Münster in 1648 at an enormous feast, a group portrait of dozens of men in their Sunday best.
Jacob Jordaens fills a canvas with gods, figures and symbols of peace to celebrate the Peace of Westphalia, the treaties of 1648 that ended the Thirty Years' War.
Rioters climb ladders to smash saints' statues and stained glass inside a church, as Protestants did during the Dutch Revolt of the 1500s.
A tall Dutch warship rams Spanish galleys off the coast of Flanders in a battle of the long Dutch fight for independence from Spain.
Dutch and Spanish fleets face each other before the Battle of the Downs in 1639, where the Dutch admiral Tromp destroyed a Spanish fleet off the English coast.
Prince Maurice of Orange leads on a white horse at the Battle of Nieuwpoort in 1600, a big Dutch victory over the Spanish in the fight for independence.
Defenders hold out in a churchyard during the Thirty Years' War, with a stormy sky overhead.
In the legend of the siege of Magdeburg in 1631, young women of the city are in desperate danger as the city falls.

events.title: The Pilgrims & Colonial America
events.summary: In 1620 the Mayflower brought about 100 English Pilgrims to Plymouth in what is now Massachusetts. With help from the Wampanoag people, they survived their first winters and shared the harvest celebration we call the first Thanksgiving. Soon more colonies grew along the Atlantic coast.
events.why: Painters of the 1800s turned the Pilgrims into America's origin story, often showing them as calm, devout and brave. Their pictures became part of how Americans remember Thanksgiving.

items.note: The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people share a harvest meal in the autumn of 1621, the event we remember as the first Thanksgiving.
The Pilgrims pray on the deck of the Speedwell in the Dutch port of Delfshaven in 1620 before sailing to America.
The Pilgrims row ashore at Plymouth in December 1620, in a famous painting by Henry Bacon of 1877.
Pilgrims walk through the snow to church, with muskets over their shoulders in case of danger.
The Mayflower, the ship that carried about 100 Pilgrims to America in 1620, rests in the harbor at sunset while a boat heads to shore.
The men of the Mayflower sign an agreement to make fair laws and govern themselves in the new colony.
Pilgrims and Wampanoag people gather for the harvest feast of 1621, which later became Thanksgiving.
Pocahontas, the daughter of the Powhatan chief, marries the English settler John Rolfe in 1614, a wedding that brought a few years of peace to Virginia.
A portrait of Pocahontas, the young Powhatan woman who became known to the English settlers at Jamestown and later traveled to England, where she died in 1617.
After being banished from the Massachusetts colony for his beliefs, Roger Williams is welcomed by Narragansett people in 1636 and founds Providence, Rhode Island, as a place of religious freedom.
Dutch settlers in the colony of New Amsterdam on Manhattan, the future New York, celebrate New Year's Day in the snow.
A young Dutch couple meets in the days when New York was still the Dutch town of New Amsterdam.
This watercolor shows the small Dutch town of New Amsterdam on the tip of Manhattan, with windmills, ships and a fort.
Pocahontas, dressed as an English lady, is presented to King James I in London in 1616.

events.title: The English Civil War
events.summary: King Charles I and Parliament went to war in 1642 over who should rule England. Oliver Cromwell's army won, and in 1649 the king was put on trial and executed. England became a republic for a few years, then brought back a king in 1660; in 1688 the Glorious Revolution settled that Parliament has the final say.
events.why: Painters loved the contrast between royal elegance and the grim fight that ended it. The scenes of Charles I's last days and Cromwell's soldiers are some of the most emotional pictures in British art.

items.note: Cavaliers and soldiers share a quiet meal and some rest before the first big battle of the English Civil War in 1642.
Oliver Cromwell leads the cavalry charge at Naseby in 1645, the battle where Parliament's New Model Army won the English Civil War.
Oliver Cromwell, the commander of the Parliament's army in the English Civil War, stands in armor with a young page beside him.
King Charles I rides a gray horse in a grand portrait by Anthony van Dyck of about 1637.
Anthony van Dyck painted the face of King Charles I from three sides in 1635 so that the sculptor Bernini in Rome could carve a bust of the king from the picture.
The five eldest children of Charles I, including the future kings Charles II and James II, stand with a huge dog in one of the sweetest royal portraits.
A small boy, the son of a Royalist, is questioned by Parliament's officers about where his father is hiding.
A hiding Royalist soldier in a hollow tree is brought food and secret messages by the girl he loves, who is on the other side of the war.
King Charles I sits quietly while his Puritan guards mock him before his trial in 1649.
A crowd gathers outside the Banqueting House in London on January 30, 1649, where King Charles I was beheaded, the only time an English king was executed.
Charles II, who was brought back as king in 1660 after eleven years without a monarch, sits in elegant robes.
In July 1690 the Protestant King William III defeated the Catholic King James II at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland, ending James's hope of getting back his throne.
King James II, who had lost his throne in the Glorious Revolution of 1688, waits on the shore for a boat to take him into exile in France.

events.title: Peter the Great & Russia Turns West
events.summary: Peter the Great, tsar of Russia from 1682 to 1725, was over six and a half feet tall and wanted his country to catch up with Europe. He traveled abroad to learn shipbuilding, defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and built a brand-new capital, Saint Petersburg, on swampy land beside the Baltic Sea.
events.why: Russian painters of the 1800s, like Repin and Serov, made Peter the star of Russian history paintings. They showed both his energy and his harshness.

items.note: Peter the Great confronts his own son, who fled abroad, in one of the most dramatic scenes of Russian history painting.
Surikov's huge canvas shows the day Peter crushed the rebellious Streltsy guards in Red Square.
Tsar Peter the Great strides ahead so fast that his courtiers struggle to keep up in this lively painting, which shows his energy and force of will.
In 1709 Peter the Great's army defeated the Swedes under Charles XII at Poltava, a victory that made Russia a great power.
In 1714 Peter the Great's new navy won its first big victory over the Swedish fleet at Gangut in the Baltic Sea.
A French painter at Peter's court, Pierre-Denis Martin, painted this view of the Battle of Poltava in 1726, only 17 years after it happened.
Swedish soldiers charge in a snowstorm at the Battle of Narva in 1700, where young King Charles XII beat the larger Russian army of Peter the Great.
Alexander Menshikov, once Peter the Great's best friend and the second most powerful man in Russia, sits in a hut in Siberia with his family after his fall from power.
Peter the Great's half-sister Sofia, who ruled Russia in his place before he took over, was locked in a convent in 1689.
Peter the Great, in armor, painted by Godfrey Kneller in 1698 while Peter was visiting England to learn about shipbuilding.
Peter the Great and his companions look over the swamp on the Neva River where he will found Saint Petersburg in 1703, a new capital that was meant to be Russia's window to Europe.

events.title: The Scientific Revolution & Enlightenment
events.summary: In the 1600s and 1700s curious people began to explore the world with experiments and reason. Galileo looked at the sky with a telescope, Newton explained gravity, and Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Diderot argued for freedom of thought. Their ideas inspired revolutions and modern science.
events.why: Painters in this age began to show scientists as heroes. Joseph Wright of Derby lit his experiments like religious scenes, as if the glow of discovery was holy.

items.note: Wright lights a science experiment like a holy scene: a bird gasps in the glass while a family decides whether to save it.
A lecturer shows a model of the solar system by candlelight, and everyone leans in to see how the planets move.
William Blake shows Isaac Newton measuring the universe with compasses, which he thought was both brilliant and too narrow.
The poet John Milton visits Galileo, who was held by the Church for saying the Earth moves around the Sun.
A crowd of writers and thinkers listens to a reading in the salon of Madame Geoffrin, one of the places where Enlightenment ideas were discussed, while a bust of Voltaire looks on.
Sir Isaac Newton, who explained gravity and the movement of the planets, looks out of this portrait by Godfrey Kneller from 1702.
Benjamin Franklin, scientist, printer and American diplomat, in a portrait painted in Paris in 1785 by Joseph-Siffred Duplessis.
Benjamin Franklin raises a hand to catch lightning from the sky, while cherubs bring electricity into the room.
At the front of the great French Encyclopédie, Truth is unveiled by Reason and Philosophy, with the light of knowledge shining.
Denis Diderot, the editor of the Encyclopédie, which tried to collect all of human knowledge in one set of books.
King Louis XIV visits the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris in 1671, where telescopes, globes and instruments show how science was becoming an official part of French life.
Alexander von Humboldt, the scientist who explored South America and described the planet as an interconnected whole, sits with his notebooks after a five-year journey.
The philosopher Aristotle, dressed in rich 1600s clothes, rests a hand on a bust of the poet Homer and seems lost in thought about wisdom, fame and money.

events.title: The Seven Years' War & the End of New France
events.summary: France and Britain fought for control of North America in the Seven Years' War (1756–1763). In 1759 British soldiers under General James Wolfe climbed cliffs near Quebec City and won a short battle on the Plains of Abraham, though both Wolfe and the French commander Montcalm were killed. France gave up Canada, and the map of North America changed.
events.why: Benjamin West's 'Death of General Wolfe' made the battle famous and started a trend of showing modern heroes in realistic clothes. Canadians and Americans still see this moment in his picture.

items.note: General Wolfe dies at the moment of victory on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec City in 1759, and West painted the scene in the clothes of his own day instead of Roman togas.
West shows a scene from the French and Indian War where a British general stops an attack on a wounded French officer.
British ships and soldiers burn an Acadian settlement on the Saint John River in 1758, during the Seven Years' War.
The French commander Montcalm, mortally wounded on the Plains of Abraham, is carried back into Quebec City on horseback in 1759.
After the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive of the East India Company meets Mir Jafar, the Indian ruler he helped put in power, in a scene from the global Seven Years' War.

Frederick the Great of Prussia is badly defeated by the Russians and Austrians at the Battle of Kunersdorf on August 1, 1759, in the Seven Years' War, which was fought in Europe, India and North America.
British warships capture the French ships Alcide and Lys off the coast of Canada in 1755, in the sea fight that helped start the Seven Years' War.
British sailors set fire to the French warship Prudent in the harbor of Louisbourg in 1758, when the British captured the fortress, a key step toward taking Quebec.
George Washington, in the red and blue uniform of a Virginia militia colonel, in a portrait painted in 1772 by Charles Willson Peale.
After Pontiac's War, Colonel Henry Bouquet forced the Native nations to hand back the settlers they had taken, and many of the captives, who had grown up with Native families, did not want to leave.
A British trading fort stands on the shore of Lake Ontario at Oswego, New York, which the French captured in 1756 early in the Seven Years' War.
British boats land at the foot of the cliffs below Quebec in 1759, before the soldiers climbed up to the Plains of Abraham to fight the French.

events.title: The American Revolution
events.summary: In 1775 American colonists began fighting for freedom from Britain. On July 4, 1776 they declared independence, and after eight years of war, led by George Washington and helped by France, they won. The United States was born as a republic where leaders are chosen by the people.
events.why: American painters, especially John Trumbull, were eager to show the founding to the world. Many of these scenes became so famous they are on money and in school books.

items.note: Trumbull's famous painting shows the Committee of Five presenting the Declaration of Independence to the Congress in 1776.
On Christmas night 1776, Washington's army crosses an icy river for a surprise attack on Trenton.
British troops lay down their arms at Yorktown in 1781, the battle that ended the war.
Burgoyne's army surrenders at Saratoga in 1777, the turning point that convinced France to join the Americans.
Charles Willson Peale, who fought in the war, shows Washington leading at the Battle of Princeton.
West's unfinished painting of the American peace negotiators in Paris, who left a blank space where the British refused to sit.
On June 17, 1775, British troops stormed Bunker Hill outside Boston, one of the first big battles of the American Revolution, and the American general Joseph Warren was killed.
George Washington and the young French marquis de Lafayette ride through the snow at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777–1778, when the American army nearly starved but became a stronger force.
British soldiers fire into a crowd in Boston on March 5, 1770, killing five colonists.
The silversmith Paul Revere, later famous for his midnight ride in 1775, rests his chin on his hand in front of a gleaming teapot.
American and British cavalry fight in a sword duel at the Battle of Cowpens in South Carolina in 1781, one of the clearest American victories of the Revolution.
The Marquis de Lafayette, a young French nobleman, joined Washington's army at the age of 19 and became a hero of the American Revolution.
Thomas Jefferson, the writer of the Declaration of Independence and the third president of the United States, was painted by Rembrandt Peale in 1800, the year Jefferson was elected.
George Washington, the leader of the American army in the Revolution and first president, in a portrait by Gilbert Stuart painted in 1803.
General George Washington on his horse watches his soldiers cross the icy Delaware River on Christmas night, 1776, before their surprise attack on Trenton.

events.title: The French Revolution
events.summary: In 1789 the people of France rose up against the king and the old system of privilege. They stormed the Bastille prison, wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and executed King Louis XVI in 1793. A time of terror followed, and the revolution ended when Napoleon took power in 1799.
events.why: Jacques-Louis David was both a painter and a revolutionary, and his pictures turned politics into art. Later artists like Delacroix made liberty itself look like a heroine.

items.note: In June 1789 the deputies of the Third Estate swear not to leave until France has a constitution.
Delacroix's Liberty carries the tricolor over a barricade. It is about the 1830 uprising, but it became the image of the whole revolutionary spirit.
David painted his friend, the revolutionary journalist Marat, murdered in his bathtub, as a kind of martyr.
On July 14, 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, a day that became the symbol of the French Revolution.
Queen Marie Antoinette sits with her children in a portrait meant to make people see her as a loving mother, after the public had turned against her.
On September 20, 1792, the French revolutionary army, mostly new volunteers, stopped the experienced Prussian army at Valmy and saved the Revolution.
King Louis XVI was beheaded in front of a large crowd in Paris on January 21, 1793, when the revolutionaries turned from reform to ending the monarchy.
Louis XVI is brought back to Paris in a carriage in 1791 after he tried to flee the country, while the crowd watches in silence.
In June 1791 the royal family, trying to escape France in disguise, was recognized and stopped by villagers in the town of Varennes.
On July 14, 1790, the first anniversary of the Bastille, hundreds of thousands of people crowd the Champ de Mars in Paris to celebrate the new France in a festival of unity.
Charlotte Corday, a young woman from Caen, stabbed the revolutionary journalist Jean-Paul Marat in his bath in July 1793 because she believed he was leading France into terror.
Antoine Lavoisier, called the father of modern chemistry, sits in a detail from a double portrait by Jacques-Louis David in 1788.
On August 10, 1792, the people of Paris attacked the Tuileries Palace, the king's home, and the monarchy fell.
Louis XVI is put on trial before the National Convention in December 1792, with the huge hall packed with deputies.

events.title: Napoleon & the Napoleonic Wars
events.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from a Corsican officer to emperor of France in 1804. His armies won huge victories at Austerlitz and Jena but failed in Russia in 1812, and he was finally beaten at Waterloo in 1815 and exiled to Saint Helena. His laws and ideas still shape Europe.
events.why: Napoleon hired the greatest painters of his age to make him look like a god-hero, while others, like Goya, painted what his wars really did to people.

items.note: Napoleon crowns himself and then his wife Josephine in Notre-Dame in 1804. David was there, sketching.
Young General Bonaparte leads the charge at Arcole in 1796, the picture that made his legend.
Delaroche shows Napoleon crossing the Alps on a mule, the realistic cousin of David's heroic version.
After the coronation, Napoleon hands out the eagle banners to his regiments.
Goya's answer to Napoleon's army: a firing squad in Madrid executes Spanish citizens.
The people of Madrid rise up against French troops in the uprising that began the Peninsular War.
Turner paints the 1805 sea battle where Nelson's fleet destroyed the French and Spanish ships.
Benjamin West shows Admiral Nelson dying on his flagship at the moment of victory.
Napoleon walks through the snow with his frozen, starving army in the winter of 1812, after taking Moscow but being unable to win the war.
Napoleon watches the huge Battle of Borodino in 1812 from a hill, looking small and uncertain among his generals.
Napoleon on horseback directs his army at Austerlitz on December 2, 1805, where he won his greatest victory against the Russians and Austrians.
Armored French cavalry charge up the slope at the Battle of Waterloo on June 18, 1815, the battle where Napoleon was finally defeated.
In November 1812, Napoleon's army fights to cross the freezing Berezina River in Russia as it retreats.
Arthur Wellesley, the Duke of Wellington, the British general who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo, in a portrait by Thomas Lawrence of 1815 in his scarlet uniform.

events.title: The Industrial Revolution
events.summary: From about 1760, steam engines, iron, coal and factories changed how people worked, traveled and lived. Railways crossed continents, cities exploded in size and goods that were once made by hand came pouring out of machines. It made some people rich and left many in smoky, crowded towns.
events.why: Artists were amazed and troubled by the new world. Turner painted a steam train racing through rain, while others showed the glow of ironworks, the hard work of laborers and the beauty of bridges.

items.note: Turner dissolves a speeding steam train into golden mist. It was a new world, painted as blurry as it felt.
Manet paints a woman and child by the railing above the Gare Saint-Lazare, with the train's steam behind them.
Van Gogh paints a train steaming across fields, the old and new worlds side by side.
A glowing spirit of Progress carries a telegraph wire across the West, with trains and settlers following.
Steam from a train fills the glass-roofed Gare Saint-Lazare in Paris in this painting by Claude Monet.
Monet turns a busy train station into a cloud of blue and gray steam and sunlight.
A train crosses a bridge over the Seine at Argenteuil, a village near Paris where the railway brought city people for weekends.
The furnaces of the ironworks at Coalbrookdale in England glow red against the night sky, in a picture of the place where the Industrial Revolution is said to have begun.
Smoking chimneys and a factory stand beside a quiet canal in this early German picture of industry, painted by Carl Blechen in 1830.
Queen Victoria opens the Great Exhibition in the giant glass Crystal Palace in London on May 1, 1851, a world fair full of machines and inventions.
Steamships and tugboats crowd a busy harbor in the French city of Rouen, with smoke rising into a hazy sky.
Smoking factory chimneys rise over green fields in Clichy, on the edge of Paris, in a painting by Vincent van Gogh of 1887.
A steam train rolls into a little suburban station in south London while the painter Camille Pissarro, who was staying in England to escape the Franco-Prussian War, looked on.
A Royal Mail coach is loaded onto a railway truck so that it can travel by train, a sign that railways were replacing horses.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert open the Great Exhibition in the Crystal Palace in 1851, with thousands of guests looking on.
Steelworkers pour white-hot metal in a Belgian steelworks in a glowing picture by Constantin Meunier of about 1885.
A coal mine with its winding towers stands in the flat landscape of County Durham in northern England.
Three men hammer a glowing piece of iron in a dark smithy in one of Goya's late paintings, a celebration of strength and hard work.

events.title: Independence & Revolutions (1820–1848)
events.summary: Between 1820 and 1848, waves of revolt swept across the world. Greeks fought for independence from the Ottoman Empire, South American countries from Spain, and in 1830 and 1848 the people of France and much of Europe rose up for more freedom. Many of these revolutions failed at first, but their ideas about nations and rights did not go away.
events.why: Romantic artists took sides. Delacroix painted Greeks suffering at Chios and Liberty marching over barricades, and artists in Latin America celebrated their own heroes like Simón Bolívar.

items.note: The 1830 July Revolution toppled the French king in three days, and Delacroix's Liberty became its symbol.
Delacroix shows Greece as a grieving woman on the ruins of Missolonghi, a call to Europe to help the Greek war for independence.
Delacroix's painting of an Ottoman attack on the Greek island of Chios stirred sympathy for Greek independence across Europe.
Brazil declares independence from Portugal in 1822: Prince Pedro raises his sword on the banks of the Ipiranga stream.
Belgians fight in the streets of Brussels in 1830, the revolt that created an independent Belgium.
Revolutionaries fight behind a barricade in a Paris street during the June Days of 1848, in one of the revolutions that swept through Europe that year.
The famous English poet Lord Byron is welcomed at Missolonghi in Greece in January 1824, when he came to help the Greek war for independence.
In October 1827 a British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman and Egyptian ships at Navarino, a sea battle that turned the Greek War of Independence in favor of the Greeks.
Hungarian cavalry fight Austrian troops at Komárom in 1849, during the Hungarian Revolution against the Habsburg Empire.
Crowds and soldiers clash in the streets of Stockholm during the March Unrest of 1848, a Swedish echo of the revolutions across Europe.
A fighter holds a barricade in Milan during the Five Days of March 1848, when the people rose up and drove the Austrian army out of the city for a time.
A cartoon from 1848 mocks the Prussian King Frederick William IV, who said he would not allow a written constitution to come between him and his people.
On December 14, 1825, Russian officers led their soldiers into Senate Square in Saint Petersburg to demand reforms after the death of the tsar, but the revolt was crushed.
Courbet's two laborers on a dusty road were the radical new subject of 1848: ordinary working people shown without prettying them up.

events.title: The Unification of Italy & Germany
events.summary: Italy and Germany were once collections of small states. In the 1800s patriots like Garibaldi, Cavour and Bismarck joined them into single nations: Italy by 1861 (with Rome in 1870), and Germany in 1871, when its emperor was crowned in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
events.why: Painters of both countries made heroic pictures to build national pride. Garibaldi's red-shirted volunteers and the German imperial proclamation became symbols of a new national identity.

items.note: On January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the German princes proclaim King Wilhelm I of Prussia Emperor of Germany, with Bismarck in white at the center.
Hayez's lovers kiss in medieval costume. Italians of 1859 read it as a hidden message about uniting against Austria.
Prussian infantry advance across the fields at Königgrätz in 1866, the battle where Prussia defeated Austria and took the lead in uniting Germany.
The captured French emperor Napoleon III sits with the Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck after the Battle of Sedan in September 1870, the defeat that ended the French Empire.
Count Camillo Benso di Cavour, the prime minister of Piedmont, was the clever politician who helped unite Italy in the 1860s.
The Italian hero Giuseppe Garibaldi is wounded in 1862 at Aspromonte while trying to march on Rome, and his red-shirted followers gather around him.
French and Italian troops defeat the Austrian army at Magenta in 1859, one of the first big victories in the war that began Italy's unification.
The Battle of Solferino in 1859 was so bloody that a Swiss businessman who witnessed it, Henry Dunant, started the Red Cross.
Italy's first national parliament is opened in 1861 under a canopy of flags and cheering crowds, when the Kingdom of Italy was officially born.
Goffredo Mameli, the young poet who wrote the words of Italy's national anthem, died at the age of 21 defending the Roman Republic in 1849.
Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian chancellor who united Germany under Prussia in 1871, in a portrait of 1890 by Franz von Lenbach.
Garibaldi's volunteers, the Thousand, storm a hill at Calatafimi in Sicily in May 1860 and beat a larger Neapolitan army, a key victory on the way to uniting Italy.

events.title: The Crimean War
events.summary: From 1853 to 1856, Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia in the Crimea, on the Black Sea. It is remembered for the doomed Charge of the Light Brigade, for Florence Nightingale's nursing and as one of the first wars photographed. Many more soldiers died of disease than of wounds.
events.why: Crimea was the first war the public could follow in newspapers, photographs and paintings. Pictures like 'The Thin Red Line' and 'Balaclava' made ordinary soldiers into heroes.

items.note: The 93rd Highlanders stand in a thin line against the Russian cavalry at Balaclava on October 25, 1854, refusing to retreat, and a newspaper called it the 'thin red line'.
The Russian navy sets the Ottoman fleet ablaze at Sinop in November 1853, a night battle that helped bring about the Crimean War.
French and British soldiers climb the hills above the Alma River on September 20, 1854, the first big battle of the Crimean War.
Eugène Lami paints the Battle of the Alma in 1855 with a wide, pale view of the hills where the French and British armies attacked Russian positions.
After a long siege, the Ottoman fortress of Kars surrendered to the Russians in November 1855 after its defenders ran out of food.
On October 25, 1854, British light cavalry rode straight down a valley into Russian cannons in the Charge of the Light Brigade, immortalized in Tennyson's poem.
French soldiers plant the tricolor flag on the Malakoff tower on September 8, 1855, the attack that finally brought down Sevastopol.
French troops fight hand-to-hand in the trenches of the Malakoff fortress in September 1855 in the final attack on Sevastopol.
Tired, silent Grenadier Guards trudge back after the Battle of Inkerman in 1854.
The Russian painter Grigory Shukaev shows the defense of Sevastopol during the long siege of 1854 and 1855, one of the longest sieges of the Crimean War.
Alexey Bogolyubov paints the burning ships of the Battle of Sinop in 1860, a few years after the Russian navy destroyed the Ottoman fleet there in 1853.
A wide view of the cavalry battle at Balaklava in October 1854, drawn by William Simpson, who traveled with the army to the Crimea as a war artist.

events.title: Slavery & the Fight for Freedom
events.summary: For hundreds of years, millions of Africans were taken across the Atlantic and forced into slavery. Brave people, from enslaved fighters like Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass to campaigners like William Wilberforce, worked to end it. Britain ended the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire in 1833, and the United States ended slavery in 1865.
events.why: Some artists used their work to make people feel the cruelty of slavery, like Turner's wild 'Slave Ship'. Others later honored the escape and the long fight for freedom.

items.note: Turner's glowing sunset hides a terrible event: slave traders throwing their human cargo overboard during a storm.
Delegates from many countries pack a London hall at the World Anti-Slavery Convention of 1840, where women were not allowed to take part, an event that helped start the women's rights movement.
A family of enslaved people flee on horseback in the early light of the Civil War.
President Lincoln reads the first draft of the Emancipation Proclamation to his cabinet in July 1862.
Crowds cheer in the French colonies as slavery is abolished on April 27, 1848, with a flag raised and people embracing.
A white woman visits former slaves on a plantation in Virginia after the Civil War, and the women's faces show different feelings.
President Abraham Lincoln, who led the Union during the Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation, sits deep in thought in this 1869 portrait by George P.
Jean-Baptiste Belley, a former slave who became a deputy to the French National Convention for Saint-Domingue (now Haiti), leans on a bust of an antislavery writer.
Thomas Clarkson, who gathered evidence against the slave trade and traveled across Britain to campaign for abolition, sits writing in this portrait painted in 1788.
People who have been enslaved are held for sale at a market in Brazil, which received more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas.
A circular scene in the center shows a Black family at home in freedom, surrounded by scenes of slavery on one side and a hopeful future on the other.
Harriet Beecher Stowe, whose novel Uncle Tom's Cabin of 1852 sold millions of copies and made many Northerners see the cruelty of slavery, in a portrait painted in 1853 by Alanson Fisher.
Gérôme shows a slave market in the Ottoman world, a scene that was meant to shock Western viewers.

events.title: The American Civil War
events.summary: From 1861 to 1865 the United States fought a terrible civil war between the Union and the slaveholding Confederacy. Abraham Lincoln's Union won, ended slavery and kept the country together, but about 620,000 soldiers died. Photography let people see the war's reality for the first time.
events.why: Winslow Homer began as a war illustrator and made some of the most honest pictures of Civil War soldiers. Other artists painted Lincoln, the great battles and the last days of the war.

items.note: Lincoln, Grant, Sherman and Admiral Porter plan the end of the war aboard a steamboat in 1865.
Union and Confederate soldiers clash at Antietam on September 17, 1862, the bloodiest single day in American history.
The Union army holds a long ridge while the Confederates attack across the fields at Gettysburg in July 1863, the turning point of the Civil War.
Soldiers fight through smoke and trees at the Battle of Shiloh in Tennessee in April 1862, an early and very bloody battle of the Civil War.
Confederate soldiers cross a wide field in Pickett's Charge, the last big attack at Gettysburg on July 3, 1863, which failed.
In March 1862 the ironclad warships Monitor and Virginia fought the first battle between armored ships, changing sea warfare forever.
Cannon fire lights up Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor on April 12, 1861, the first shots of the American Civil War.
General William Tecumseh Sherman's Union army marches across Georgia in 1864, destroying railroads and supplies to break the Confederacy.
Union ships under Admiral Farragut steam into Mobile Bay in August 1864, where he is said to have shouted 'Damn the torpedoes!' Julian Davidson made this color print in 1886.
A Union line holds against waves of Confederate attackers at the Battle of Franklin in Tennessee in 1864, one of the last big Confederate attacks of the war.
Mathew Brady took this photograph of Abraham Lincoln in New York on the day he made his famous Cooper Union speech in February 1860.
Timothy O'Sullivan photographed the battlefield at Gettysburg in July 1863, showing the true cost of the war.
Confederate and Union soldiers fight in the woods at Chickamauga, Georgia, in September 1863, one of the largest and bloodiest battles of the Civil War in the West.

events.title: Westward Expansion & the Frontier
events.summary: In the 1800s settlers, miners, railroads and cowboys moved across North America to the Pacific. The Louisiana Purchase, the Oregon Trail, the Gold Rush and the Transcontinental Railroad opened the West, while Indigenous nations lost their lands, often by force. In Canada, a railroad stitched the country together after Confederation in 1867.
events.why: Artists like Albert Bierstadt and Frederic Remington created the American West as a place of mountains, wagon trains, cowboys and epic skies, a picture that still shapes how we imagine it.

items.note: In Gast's famous picture, a gigantic glowing figure floats over the West carrying schoolbooks and a telegraph wire, with railroads and wagons following.
Leutze's mural for the US Capitol shows pioneers reaching the crest of the Rockies and seeing the Pacific.
The leaders who created Canada in 1867 meet in Quebec. The painting hung in Parliament until it was destroyed by fire in 1916.
Tipis stand by a trading fort in Wyoming, where trappers and Native American traders met and where the Oregon Trail passed.
The frontiersman Daniel Boone leads a group of pioneers through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky, with a woman riding a white horse.
The explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, who crossed the continent in 1804 to 1806, meet the Salish people at Ross' Hole in what is now Montana.
On May 10, 1869, the last spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads at Promontory, Utah, creating the first railroad across America.
Wagons wind through a glowing landscape under a red sky on the Oregon Trail, the long route that tens of thousands of settlers took west.
Daniel Boone and his friends look out over the green land of Kentucky for the first time in 1769, in a painting that made the frontier look wide open.
Cowboys, also called buckaroos, ride in the open West in this lively painting by Charles M.
Two cowboys race on horses to catch a runaway steer, in a scene full of speed and dust.
Thousands of Chinese workers built the Central Pacific Railroad through the Sierra Nevada, digging tunnels and clearing rock by hand, in very dangerous conditions.
In June 1876 the Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated General Custer's soldiers at the Battle of the Little Bighorn, one of the greatest victories for Native Americans in the Plains Wars.

events.title: The Franco-Prussian War & the Paris Commune
events.summary: In 1870 France declared war on Prussia and lost quickly. Emperor Napoleon III was captured at Sedan, Paris was besieged and starved for four months, and Germany became an empire.
