Then Parisians rose in a short-lived revolt called the Paris Commune, which was crushed in a week of bloody fighting.
events.why: French painters like Meissonier and Detaille turned the defeat into pictures of courage, loss and hope for revenge. Their huge, detailed canvases are history lessons you can walk into.

items.note: Paris, personified as a woman holding a flag, rises among dead soldiers during the German siege of the French capital in the winter of 1870 and 1871.
French troops attack in the snow at Champigny in December 1870, trying to break out of besieged Paris.
French armored cavalry charge through the narrow streets of the village of Morsbronn on August 6, 1870, in a brave but hopeless attack against Prussian infantry.
French soldiers defend a village cemetery at Saint-Privat against German attackers during the Franco-Prussian War in August 1870.
The worn-out French army of General Bourbaki, starved and half frozen, crosses into Switzerland in February 1871 to escape the Germans, and Swiss people took the soldiers in.
On January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the German princes proclaim King Wilhelm I of Prussia Emperor of Germany, with Bismarck in white at the center.
German officers rest in a smart French parlor during the siege of Paris, one with his boots on the table beside a piano.
The captured French emperor Napoleon III sits with the Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck after the Battle of Sedan in September 1870, the defeat that ended the French Empire.
French General Louis Faidherbe rides on a white horse at the Battle of Bapaume in January 1871, one of the few French successes in the late war.
The great Paris city hall, the Hôtel de Ville, burns on May 24, 1871, during the last week of the Paris Commune, the radical government of Paris.
Louise Michel, a teacher who fought for the Paris Commune, is arrested by soldiers in 1871 and later sent to a prison colony in the Pacific.
A young woman in white sits among ruins, holding a green branch, as a symbol of hope after France's defeat in the war of 1870 and 1871.
Soldiers shoot captured members of the Paris Commune at the Lobau Barracks in May 1871, during the 'Bloody Week' that ended the Commune.

events.title: Votes for Women
events.summary: For centuries women were not allowed to vote. In 1848 a meeting at Seneca Falls, New York, called for women's rights, and campaigns grew in Britain, the United States and Scandinavia. New Zealand allowed women to vote in 1893, Norway in 1913, Canada from 1917 to 1919 and the United States in 1920.
events.why: Posters, banners and paintings were important weapons for the suffrage movement. Colorful art turned a hard political fight into pictures that anyone could understand.

items.note: A colorful program for the great Woman Suffrage Procession held in Washington on March 3, 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson became president.
A woman in a golden gown, a symbol of Liberty, strides across a map of the United States in which the states where women could vote glow in gold.
Lucretia Mott, a Quaker minister and abolitionist, was one of the organizers of the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, which launched the American women's rights movement.
A cartoon by Nina Allender, the cartoonist of Alice Paul's National Woman's Party, shows suffragists behind bars after being arrested for picketing outside the White House in 1917.
A woman and a child stand in front of the Capitol on a poster for the League of Women Voters.
A map of North America, with the states and provinces where women could vote marked, on a suffrage poster from 1917.
A Life magazine cover from the suffrage-themed issue of February 1913, in black and gold, by Rea Irvin, who later designed the New Yorker's first cover.
A map shows in yellow the states where women already had equal suffrage in 1915, and the poster urges voters to approve the woman suffrage amendment in November.
An anti-suffrage poster from 1915, made by opponents of women voting, borrows the title of a famous song.
Police carry the British suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst away on May 21, 1914, after she tried to bring a petition to King George V at Buckingham Palace.
Nellie McClung, the Canadian writer and activist who led the campaign that made Manitoba the first province to give women the vote in 1916.
Women's Social and Political Union leaders meet around 1906.
Millicent Fawcett, the leader of Britain's peaceful suffrage societies, sits with her niece Louisa Garrett Anderson.

events.title: World War I
events.summary: World War I (1914–1918) pulled in most of the world's great powers and was fought in muddy trenches from Belgium to Russia and across the seas. New weapons like machine guns, poison gas and airplanes made it deadlier than any earlier war. Around 20 million people died, and it was called 'the war to end all wars'.
events.why: Official war artists were sent to the front, and many returned with unforgettable pictures of soldiers, wrecked landscapes and the strange beauty of battlefields.

items.note: Sargent painted blinded soldiers, with bandaged eyes, walking in a line toward a field hospital after a mustard gas attack.
Orpen painted the peace treaty that ended the war being signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in 1919.
Australian and New Zealand troops scramble ashore at Gallipoli in April 1915.
A Canadian painter records the joyful crowds on November 11, 1918, when the guns finally stopped.
A broken, twisted forest of shattered tree stumps stands in a landscape ripped by shell craters, under a bitter-sounding title.
Paul Nash paints a wrecked, muddy landscape near Ypres in Belgium, with flooded craters and splintered trees.
A.Y.
A bare, shell-torn hill called the Pimple glows red in the evening light near Vimy Ridge, where Canadian troops had fought in 1917.
Canadian gunners push and pull an artillery piece through deep mud at Passchendaele in late 1917, one of the worst battles of the war.
A print of a cemetery on Vimy Ridge, the French hill where Canadian soldiers won a famous victory in April 1917.
A single aeroplane sails among huge clouds in a dreamy, modern view of the war in the sky.
Women work in a roaring factory filling shells for the war effort in 1918.
Soldiers gather in a candlelit American Red Cross canteen at the front in France.
Wyndham Lewis shows an artillery position under fire in sharp, blocky shapes, like a machine of broken glass.
Ghostly soldiers rise out of the fields near the Menin Gate, the great memorial at Ypres to the missing of World War I.
A huge crater from a mine explosion and a lonely grave mark the old battlefield at La Boisselle, on the Somme.
The Australian war artist Arthur Streeton paints the soft green countryside around Amiens, the city that the Allies defended and then used for their big attack of August 1918.

events.title: The Russian Revolution
events.summary: In 1917 Russia's tsar was overthrown in the February Revolution, and in October the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power. A civil war followed, and in 1922 the Soviet Union was formed. The revolution changed Russia, and for most of the 1900s it also shaped world politics.
events.why: Artists were part of the revolution. Posters, banners and bold new styles were used to explain the new world, while painters like Kustodiev recorded the crowds in the streets.

items.note: A huge worker holding a red flag strides over the crowded rooftops of a Russian city in this symbol of the Bolshevik revolution.
Crowds joyfully wave flags and red banners in the streets after Tsar Nicholas II promised civil rights and a parliament in October 1905.
Ilya Repin's lively early study for his painting of the crowds celebrating Tsar Nicholas II's October Manifesto of 1905, with swirls of red flags.
Soldiers and workers rush into the Winter Palace, the home of the Russian government, on the night of October 25, 1917, when the Bolsheviks seized power.
Vladimir Lenin, the leader of the Bolshevik Revolution, lies in his coffin surrounded by red flags and officials in January 1924.
A red triangle slices into a white circle in El Lissitzky's famous poster, a symbol of the Red Army defeating the White Army in the Russian Civil War.
A Soviet poster of 1920 uses bold colors and cartoon figures in the style of the revolution's propaganda posters, which taught people about the new government in a country where many could not read.
A poster compares life before October 1917 and after it, using simple pictures so that everyone could understand the Bolshevik message.
On January 22, 1905, soldiers fired on peaceful workers marching to the Winter Palace to ask the tsar for help, killing and wounding many, an event that started the Revolution of 1905.
Malevich's Red Square, made in 1915, is one of the first pictures with no objects at all, a bold new art for a country about to remake itself.
Malevich pushes his revolution in art as far as it goes: a white square on a white ground, painted the year after the revolution.
Malevich's Black Square, shown in 1915, announced that painting could start from zero, just as Russia was about to.

events.title: The Great Depression
events.summary: After the stock market crash of 1929, millions of people lost their jobs and savings. In the United States, the Dust Bowl blew away farmers' soil, and President Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal created work programs that built roads, parks and post offices, and hired artists to paint murals and take photographs.
events.why: The government hired photographers like Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans to document hard times. Their pictures are now treasured as art, and they show people with great dignity.

items.note: Florence Owens Thompson sits in a pea-pickers' camp in California in 1936, with her children turned away.
A farmer and his sons walk bent against a huge dust cloud in Oklahoma in April 1936, during the Dust Bowl.

A man and woman carry their bags along an empty road in California in 1937, with a billboard above them that says 'Next time try the train.' Dorothea Lange's photo shows the ordeal of families who moved west to look for work.
An empty farmhouse stands in a wide field of plowed furrows in Texas in 1938, a farm where tractors had taken the place of families who once worked the land as tenant farmers.
An elderly woman in Alabama who was born into slavery stands in front of her house in 1938.
Allie Mae Burroughs, the wife of a cotton sharecropper, looks straight at the camera in 1936.
Three cotton sharecroppers sit together on a porch in Alabama in 1936.
Floyd Burroughs, a cotton sharecropper in Alabama, looks into the camera in 1936.
Jim Norris, a homesteader in Pie Town, New Mexico, in 1940, photographed in rare color film by Russell Lee for the government.
Children sing together in a school in Pie Town, New Mexico, in 1940, in a color photograph by Russell Lee.
Ella Watson, a cleaning woman at a government office, stands with a mop and broom in front of an American flag in 1942.
A poster from the Works Progress Administration, the New Deal program that put millions of Americans back to work building roads, bridges and schools, as well as paying artists and writers.
Ella Watson with her family at home in Washington, D.C., in 1942, in a photograph by Gordon Parks.

events.title: World War II
events.summary: World War II (1939–1945) was the largest war in history, fought across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific. The Allies, including the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and Canada, defeated Nazi Germany, Italy and Japan. The war included the Holocaust, in which six million Jews were murdered, and ended with the atomic bombs on Japan and the creation of the United Nations.
events.why: The US Army and Navy sent artists to the front lines to record the war. These paintings and drawings, which belong to the American people, show soldiers, sailors and the home front.

items.note: Trucks and landing craft sit on a muddy beach in the Netherlands in 1945, painted by the Canadian war artist Alex Colville.
The great steel bridge at Nijmegen, which the Allies captured in September 1944 in the failed Operation Market Garden, arches across the river.
Army trucks roll along a road in the green hills of Yorkshire, England, where Canadian soldiers trained in 1944 before D-Day.
Landing craft head toward the coast in the Allied invasion of southern France in August 1944, in a painting by the Canadian war artist Alex Colville.
A Canadian tank rolls through the shattered streets of Ortona, Italy, where Canadian troops fought a fierce street battle in December 1943.
Flares and searchlights light up the sky over the Italian hills before an attack on the Hitler Line in 1944.
A line of Canadian tanks rolls over a green landscape in 1944.
Women of the Canadian Women's Army Corps play in a brass band in 1945.
A dark London street during the wartime blackout, when all lights were turned off so that bombers could not find the city.
An LVT, a tracked amphibious vehicle, drives up a beach on Saipan in June 1944 during the fighting in the Pacific.
Landing boats, soldiers and equipment fill Utah Beach in Normandy after the D-Day landings of June 6, 1944.
On September 2, 1945, aboard the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Japanese officials signed the surrender that ended World War II.
Ground crews load Vultee Vengeance dive-bombers in a busy scene from the war.
American soldiers crouch among tropical trees during an assault in the Pacific in 1943.
A sailor strains to load a big gun aboard a navy ship in 1940 in a powerful, poster-like painting.
A quiet field with open pits near the huts of Bergen-Belsen shows the horror of the Nazi concentration camp, which British and Canadian troops reached in April 1945.
Fire sweeps through a battlefield in the Pacific in 1944 in a painting by William F.

events.title: The Space Race & the Moon Landing
events.summary: In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, and the Space Race began. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, and on July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of Apollo 11 became the first people to walk on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve Americans walked on the Moon in all.
events.why: NASA photographs from the Moon are some of the most famous images of all time, and they count as art too: Earthrise and the Blue Marble changed how people see our planet.

items.note: Buzz Aldrin stands on the Moon on July 20, 1969, in a photograph taken by Neil Armstrong, whose reflection you can see in Aldrin's gold visor.

Our blue Earth rises over the gray edge of the Moon in this photograph taken by astronaut William Anders on Christmas Eve 1968 during Apollo 8, the first time people had seen the whole Earth from another world.
The whole Earth, round and blue and shining, photographed by the Apollo 17 astronauts on their way to the Moon in December 1972.
A Saturn V rocket rises on a pillar of fire and smoke at the Kennedy Space Center on July 16, 1969, carrying the Apollo 11 crew to the Moon.
Astronaut Alan Shepard sits in the tiny Freedom 7 capsule before his flight on May 5, 1961, when he became the first American in space.
A single bootprint in the gray Moon dust, taken by the Apollo 11 astronauts to study the lunar soil.
Buzz Aldrin looks back at the landing site, Tranquility Base, in the bright gray landscape of the Moon, with the lunar module Eagle behind him.
Buzz Aldrin climbs down the ladder of the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle onto the Moon in July 1969.
Buzz Aldrin stands beside the American flag on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
The crew of Apollo 11: Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin, in their white space suits.
Astronaut James Irwin salutes the flag beside the lunar module and the moon buggy, the lunar rover, in 1971.
The huge Saturn V rocket for Apollo 11 is carried slowly toward the launch pad on a giant crawler in May 1969.

events.title: The Vietnam War
events.summary: From 1965 to 1973 the United States fought in the Vietnam War, supporting South Vietnam against the Communist North. It was a long and costly conflict at home and overseas, with huge protests in the United States, and ended with US troops leaving in 1973 and the North taking the South in 1975.
events.why: The US Army sent combat artists to Vietnam, just as it had in the world wars. Their paintings and drawings, made for the government and so in the public domain, show soldiers, helicopters and villages, and the quiet moments between the fighting.

items.note: Soldiers work on a big artillery gun in Vietnam in 1968 in a painting by David Fairrington.
A soldier carries a radio, the lifeline of a patrol, in a tall, bold painting by David Fairrington.
A soldier strides through golden grass in Vietnam in a painting of 1968 by David Fairrington.
Vietnamese women in cone-shaped hats gather in a colorful, patterned scene by David Fairrington in 1968.
Two Vietnamese girls lean close to each other in a gentle painting by David Fairrington from 1968.
A Cobra attack helicopter, one of the most important aircraft of the Vietnam War, is painted in dark glassy shapes by Stephen H.
A helicopter waits on the ground in a muddy field in Vietnam, in a watercolor by Stephen H.
Two soldiers lean over the edge of a bunker in Vietnam in a sketchy watercolor by Stephen H.
Medics treat a wounded soldier in a busy scene by Stephen H.
Medics rush a wounded soldier to a waiting helicopter in a swirl of blue, in a painting of 1967 by Ronald A.
Ronald A.
Flares light up the night sky while glowing lines of tracer fire cross the dark in this blue painting of 1967 by Ronald A.
A swirling, almost abstract picture of a trail through the jungle in Vietnam by James Pollock in 1967.
Soldiers in dark, heavy shapes struggle in a tense scene by Stephen H.
